nameStory: The Atlantic Blue Crab gets its colorful name from the stunning bright blue claws that make it instantly recognizable in New England waters. While their bodies are more olive-green to brownish, those brilliant sapphire-blue claws (especially prominent in males) create such a striking impression that 'blue crab' became the obvious choice. The scientific name 'sapidus' actually means 'savory' or 'tasty' — a clear nod to their reputation as excellent eating!
description: The Atlantic Blue Crab is a medium-sized swimming crab with a broad, flattened shell and distinctive bright blue claws. These crabs typically measure 4-9 inches across their shell and have five pairs of legs, with the back pair modified into paddle-like swimming appendages. Their shell (called a carapace) is olive-green to brown with a somewhat triangular shape, while males sport those famous brilliant blue claws. They're excellent swimmers and can move both forward and sideways with surprising speed.

idTips.label: Bright Blue Claws
idTips.description: Males have unmistakable bright sapphire-blue claws that almost seem to glow underwater — you can spot this electric blue color from several feet away, especially on sunny days

idTips.label: Paddle-Shaped Back Legs
idTips.description: The last pair of legs are flattened into oval paddles that feel firm and smooth, unlike the pointed walking legs — these swimming appendages are unique among New England crabs

idTips.label: Shell Shape and Spines
idTips.description: The shell feels hard and smooth with sharp spines along the edges that can prick your fingers if you're not careful — much more pointed than a rock crab's rounded shell

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Larger and more robust than most other New England crabs, with a substantial weight in your hands and a shell that's noticeably wider than it is long

idTips.label: Swimming Behavior
idTips.description: Unlike other crabs that mainly scuttle along the bottom, these actively swim through the water column using their paddle legs — watch for their distinctive sideways swimming motion

habitat: In New England, Atlantic Blue Crabs prefer shallow coastal waters, especially around salt marshes, tidal creeks, and protected bays with sandy or muddy bottoms. They're commonly found in eelgrass beds and areas where fresh water mixes with salt water, such as river mouths and estuaries. Look for them in depths from just a few feet to about 30 feet, often hiding among vegetation or partially buried in soft sediment.

seasonality.spring: Blue crabs begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm, making them easier to spot in tidal pools and marsh edges during May and June.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when crabs are most active and visible, often seen swimming in shallow bays and around docks. This is also mating season, so you might observe interesting behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Crabs remain active through early fall but begin moving to deeper waters as temperatures drop. September and October can still offer good viewing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Most blue crabs move to deeper waters or bury themselves in mud to hibernate, making them rarely seen during New England's cold months.

funFact: Blue crabs are incredible athletes of the sea — they can swim forward, backward, and sideways at speeds up to 5 miles per hour, and some individuals have been tracked migrating over 300 miles along the coast, with one tagged crab traveling from the Chesapeake Bay all the way to Nova Scotia!
confusionNotes: Blue crabs are sometimes confused with green crabs, but remember 'blue claws, not blue shell' — green crabs are much smaller, can't swim, and lack those distinctive bright blue claws. If you see brilliant blue claws and paddle-shaped back legs, you've found a blue crab!
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'blue' crabs, only the claws are truly blue — the body is typically olive-green or brown, which surprises many first-time observers. These crabs are actually southern visitors that have been expanding their range northward, so seeing one in New England waters is becoming more common due to warming ocean temperatures.
compareHints: Atlantic Blue Crabs are much larger than their cousin the Lesser Blue Crab, which rarely appears in New England waters and typically stays under 4 inches wide. The Atlantic Blue Crab's claws are more dramatically blue and the overall build is more robust. Unlike other swimming crabs in the same family, blue crabs have that distinctive bright blue coloration and are the only ones commonly seen in New England estuaries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the Atlantic Blue Crab, the Lesser Blue Crab is significantly smaller with a more delicate build and proportionally smaller claws.
